title: Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām: the fifth face, Īśāna
theme: The last of the five mantras on the faces of Śiva: Īśāna, ruler of all knowledge and all beings, is asked to be gracious, and the mantra closes on Sadāśiva and Om.

words.meaning: the ruler, the one who governs
words.role: first of the names in apposition
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «सर्वविद्यानामीशानो नियामकः» — the controller of all branches of knowledge
The anonymous commentator: «सर्वभूतानामखिलप्राणिनामीश्वरो नियामकः» — the controller of all living beings
The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: «ब्रह्माधिपतिर्वेदस्याधिकत्वेन पालकः» — brahman here is the Veda, which he guards as its overlord
The anonymous commentator: «ब्रह्मणो हिरण्यगर्भस्याधिपतिः» — of Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha

words.gram: m. nom. sg. (Bhāskara: neuter brahma with the vowel lengthened)
words.meaning: Brahmā — or brahman, the great one
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «तादृशो यो ब्रह्मा प्रवृद्धः परमात्मा» — such a one, the grown-great supreme self
The anonymous commentator: «शिवः शान्तोऽस्तु» — may he be gentle
The anonymous commentator: «मे ममानुग्रहाय» — for my favour

words.role: name in apposition to the subject, closing the mantra
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «स एव सदाशिव ओमहं भवामि» — that very Sadāśiva, Om, I become
Bhāskara: «सस्थाने प्रणवः» — the praṇava stands where sa (‘he’) would

sandhi.rule: A final m is joined to a following vowel: sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ.

sandhi.type: visarga after i before a voiced sound; -aḥ before a
sandhi.rule: adhipatiḥ + brahmaṇaḥ → adhipatir brahmaṇaḥ (the visarga after i becomes r before a voiced sound); brahmaṇaḥ + adhipatiḥ → brahmaṇo ’dhipatiḥ: -aḥ becomes -o before a, and the a is elided (P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)), marked by the avagraha.
-aḥ becomes -o before a voiced consonant: śivaḥ + me → śivo me.

sandhi.type: -aḥ before om: the a merges into o
sandhi.rule: The visarga falls before a vowel, and a + om gives om, the second vowel replacing the first (P. 6.1.95 (ओमाङोश्च)): sadāśivaḥ + om → sadāśivom. Bhāskara names this rule as one way to explain the form.

sandhi_exceptions.note: me · astu: the e of me is not joined to the following a (classical me ’stu). In Vedic recitation e and o before a inside a pāda keep their form (P. 6.1.115 (प्रकृत्याऽन्तःपादमव्यपरे)); every witness prints me astu.

samasa.meaning: overlord of brahman (the Veda, for the commentators)

morphology.note: Read as the masculine brahmā (Brahmā, or the supreme self ‘grown great’) by the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa. Bhāskara reads the neuter brahma, ‘the supreme reality’, and explains the long final vowel as a Vedic lengthening in the joined text: «छान्दसं सांहितिकं दीर्घत्वम्».
In the joined text the name and the following Om fuse into sadāśivom. The commentators do not agree on what the fusion means: see the commentary.

translation.literal: The ruler of all branches of knowledge, the lord of all beings, the overlord of brahman, the overlord of Brahmā — [that] Brahmā (or: brahman) — may [he be] gracious to me. Sadāśiva. Om.
translation.readable: Ruler of every kind of knowledge, lord of all that lives, guardian of the Veda, master even of Brahmā the creator: may that great one be gracious to me. He is Sadāśiva, the ever-auspicious. Om.

syntax: A string of nominatives in apposition — īśānaḥ, īśvaraḥ, brahmādhipatiḥ, adhipatiḥ, brahmā — each with its genitive, followed by a single wish, śivo me astu (‘may [he] be gracious to me’). The name sadāśivaḥ and the syllable om close the formula, fused in the joined text.

ambiguities.note: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read one compound, ‘overlord of brahman’, taking brahman as the Veda. Bhāskara divides it, brahmā adhipatiḥ: ‘the great one, overlord of all’ («ब्रह्मा सर्वात्मना परिबृढो ऽधिपतिर्»). The joined text allows both.
The masculine Brahmā (the creator, or the supreme self as ‘grown great’) or the neuter brahma with a lengthened vowel (Bhāskara). The commentators differ; the text alone does not decide.
Sadāśiva followed by Om; the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa make it a statement of identity by the reciter, Bhāskara a name with the praṇava standing for ‘he’.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A yajus formula in prose, one line of 38 syllables; no metrical division.

beginner: This short prayer is the last of five that address the five faces of Śiva, each face with its own name. The fifth face looks upward and is called Īśāna, the Ruler. The prayer piles up titles: ruler of every kind of knowledge, lord of every living being, guardian of the sacred Veda, master even of Brahmā, the creator. Then it makes one simple request: may this great one be kind to me. It ends with the name Sadāśiva, the Ever-Auspicious, and the sacred syllable Om, run together into a single sound. The old commentators read that ending in two ways: one says the reciter declares, ‘I am that Sadāśiva’; another hears Om simply taking the place of the word ‘he’. The prayer itself states what it asks; it makes no claim about what reciting it brings.
analogy: Like addressing a letter with every title of its recipient before writing a one-line request: the titles say who is asked, the line says what for.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It names one being by five titles — ruler of all knowledge, lord of all beings, overlord of brahman, overlord of Brahmā, Brahmā (or brahman) — and asks that he be gracious to the speaker. It ends with the name Sadāśiva and Om.

commentary.q: Which face of Śiva is this?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa both say the mantra sets out the upward face: «ऊर्ध्ववक्त्रप्रतिपादकं मन्त्रमाह». In this text it closes the series of five mantras on the faces of Mahādeva that begins at 10.17 (sadyojātam), which the anonymous commentator introduces as being about «महादेवसंबन्धिषु पञ्च» faces. In Sāyaṇa’s own order the five stand at his anuvākas 43–47.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator takes the brahman of brahmādhipatiḥ as the Veda and the brahman of brahmaṇaḥ as Hiraṇyagarbha: «ब्रह्मणो हिरण्यगर्भस्याधिपतिः». The final brahmā is for him the supreme self: «तादृशो यो ब्रह्मा प्रवृद्धः परमात्मा». Bhāskara reads the last word as the neuter, the supreme reality beyond the world, «ब्रह्मा विश्वाधिक परं वस्तु», with a Vedic long vowel.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: For the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa the reciter declares identity with Sadāśiva: «स एव सदाशिव ओमहं भवामि» — ‘that very Sadāśiva, Om, I become’. Bhāskara takes Sadāśiva as the god’s name, ‘the self of the praṇava’, and Om as standing where ‘he’ would: «सस्थाने प्रणवः». He adds a grammatical alternative: the joined form by P. 6.1.95 (ओमाङोश्च), «इति पररूपत्वं कृतम्».

commentary.q: How is the joined text formed?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Two junctions are unusual. me astu keeps the e of me before a, as Vedic recitation does inside a pāda (P. 6.1.115 (प्रकृत्याऽन्तःपादमव्यपरे)), where classical Sanskrit would write me ’stu. And sadāśivaḥ + om gives sadāśivom: the visarga falls before the vowel and the o of om replaces the a (P. 6.1.95 (ओमाङोश्च)).

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources: the anonymous bhāṣya, Sāyaṇa and Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara explain the mantra and its use, not a school’s doctrine (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The one real difference among them is the closing: identity with Sadāśiva for the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa, a name with the praṇava for ‘he’ for Bhāskara.

parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka calls the self within the heart ‘ruler of all, overlord of all’ — the same two titles, īśāna and adhipati, that this mantra gives Īśāna.

contemporary.text: The mantra gives its addressee every title of power — over knowledge, over beings, over the Veda, over the creator — and then asks only that he be gentle. Power named in full and then asked for kindness is a pattern worth noticing wherever authority is held: the more is held, the more the request for gentleness matters. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a prayer list so many titles before making a single, small request?
reflect.deeper: The commentators hear ‘Sadāśiva, Om’ either as the reciter’s own identity or as a name with Om standing for ‘he’. What changes in the mantra between the two readings?
reflect.practice: Read the five titles slowly, one per breath, and notice which one you linger on.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this mantra as his anuvāka 47 and Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara as his anuvāka 47; both are reached through the edition’s concordance, which maps them correctly here.

flags.note: Whether the closing sadāśivom declares the reciter’s identity with Sadāśiva (the anonymous commentator, Sāyaṇa) or names the god with Om for ‘he’ (Bhāskara) is a matter of interpretation; the text gives only the fused form.
